title: CTEs & Subqueries
interviewAnswer: CTEs make complex SQL easier to reason about by naming intermediate results. They are often used to structure transformations before the final query.
why: CTEs and subqueries test how you structure multi-step SQL and reason about readability versus optimizer behavior.
intuition: A subquery nests a query inside another expression. A CTE names an intermediate query so complex logic reads like staged transformations.
deepDive: CTEs improve organization and can be recursive. Modern optimizers may inline them, but materialization behavior is database/version specific. Correlated subqueries reference outer rows and can be expensive if not optimized. EXISTS is often a clear way to express “does any related row exist?” without duplicate joins.
workedExample: Use a CTE to aggregate order spend per customer, then join that one-row-per-customer result to customer attributes. This makes grain explicit.
commonMistakes: Assuming a CTE always materializes or is always faster.
Using SELECT * in deeply nested transformations and losing schema clarity.
Using correlated subqueries without checking the execution plan.
production: Prefer maintainable SQL with explicit grain/columns; performance decisions should come from query plans and realistic data, not blanket rules about CTEs.
